description: Public names of the package, their categories (the blocks of Development/src/00_header.wl) and the public names they use (edges from user to used). Generated by Development/make_function_map.wl.

nodes.name: IntegralOver
nodes.usage: IntegralOver[f, {x, y, ...}] is the integral (or sum) of f over the integration variables x, y, ... (space, time, spin and any other label they stand for). Integration variables must be symbols; IntegralOver[f, x] is IntegralOver[f, {x}].

nodes.name: DeltaFunction
nodes.usage: DeltaFunction[x, y] is the delta function δ(x - y) of two labels. It is symmetric and is integrated automatically against IntegralOver variables.

nodes.name: GrassmannProduct
nodes.usage: GrassmannProduct[a, b, ...] is the ordered product of Grassmann-odd factors. Products entered with ** (NonCommutativeMultiply) are converted to it.

nodes.name: DummyVariable
nodes.usage: DummyVariable[depth, k] is the k-th canonical integration variable at nesting depth depth; it is displayed as z_k (w_k, u_k, ... inside nested integrals).

nodes.name: DeclareSource
nodes.usage: DeclareSource[J1, J2, ...] declares commuting (bosonic) source heads: J[x] is then differentiated by FunctionalDerivative.

nodes.name: DeclareGrassmannSource
nodes.usage: DeclareGrassmannSource[eta, etabar, ...] declares anticommuting (Grassmann) source heads.

nodes.name: DeclareGrassmannOdd
nodes.usage: DeclareGrassmannOdd[psi, ...] declares heads of Grassmann-odd quantities that do not depend on the sources (for instance fermion fields inside an interaction).

nodes.name: DeclareGrassmannGraded
nodes.usage: DeclareGrassmannGraded[h, ...] declares heads whose Grassmann parity is the number of their arguments mod 2 and which depend on the sources (odd ones vanish at zero sources). Used by ConnectedFunctionFromVertices for fermions (superfield rules).

nodes.name: DeclareSymmetric
nodes.usage: DeclareSymmetric[h, ...] makes h totally symmetric in its arguments (for example a bosonic propagator or a density-density interaction).

nodes.name: DeclareAntisymmetric
nodes.usage: DeclareAntisymmetric[h, ...] makes h totally antisymmetric in its arguments (h[b, a] evaluates to -h[a, b], h[a, a] to 0: in a pattern or a rule write h[__], never h[_, _]). The derivative with respect to an antisymmetric kernel, FunctionalDerivative[F, h[x, y]], is antisymmetrised, and the kernel of the inverse of an antisymmetric operator, OperatorKernel[h^-1], is antisymmetric: a superfield propagator, the Nambu matrix of (psi, psibar) with the normal block G and the anomalous blocks -<T psi psi> and -<T psibar psibar>, is such a kernel.

nodes.name: DeclareFunctionalDerivative
nodes.usage: DeclareFunctionalDerivative[object[a_, ...], source[c_], rhs] declares the functional derivative δobject/δsource = rhs of an object that depends on the sources implicitly. Integration variables in rhs are renamed automatically.

nodes.name: DeclareDiscreteIndexValues
nodes.usage: DeclareDiscreteIndexValues[{up, down, ...}] declares discrete index values: DeltaFunction[up, up] = 1 and DeltaFunction[up, down] = 0.

nodes.name: DeclareField
nodes.usage: DeclareField[phi, J] associates the field phi with the source J (phi[x] stands for δ/δJ[x]); DeclareField[psibar, eta, -1] associates psibar[x] with -δ/δeta[x]. Fields attached to Grassmann sources are Grassmann odd.

nodes.name: DeclareLineStyle
nodes.usage: DeclareLineStyle[h, style] sets how a two-label factor h[x, y] is drawn: "Plain", "Arrow" (a propagator running from y to x), "DoubleArrow" (a dressed propagator), "DottedArrow" (a ghost), "Double", "Wavy", "DoubleWavy" (a dressed interaction beside the bare one, e.g. the screened W next to V), "Curly" (a gluon), "Dashed", "Dotted", "Zigzag", "Impurity" (dashed, with a cross), "DivergingArrows" (an anomalous propagator -<T psi(x) psi(y)>: two arrowheads pointing to its ends) or "ConvergingArrows" (-<T psibar(x) psibar(y)>: two arrowheads pointing to its middle). The seven from "Wavy" to "Impurity" are drawn as interaction lines; the arrows run on through every vertex and turn only inside an anomalous line.

nodes.name: DeclareDirectedPropagator
nodes.usage: DeclareDirectedPropagator[G, ...] is DeclareLineStyle[G, "Arrow"]: G[x, y] is drawn with an arrow from y to x (a fermion propagating from y to x).

nodes.name: DeclareInteractionLine
nodes.usage: DeclareInteractionLine[V, ...] declares interaction lines, kernels of the interaction such as V in S_int = 1/2 ∫ V(x, y) psibar(x) psibar(y) psi(y) psi(x): V[x, y] is drawn as a wavy line, and in the weight written with a picture it stands for -V (the minus sign comes from expanding exp(-S_int)). DeclareInteractionLine[V, ..., style] draws them in another style, e.g. "DoubleWavy" for a screened interaction W drawn beside V (in a skeleton expansion, where every line is a dressed one, the plain styles are used: the option "Interactions" -> {W} draws W as a wavy line in one picture). A line declared only with DeclareLineStyle is a propagator and stands for itself.

nodes.name: DeclareCoupling
nodes.usage: DeclareCoupling[lambda, ...] declares couplings of local interactions, such as lambda in S_int = lambda/4! ∫ phi^4 or g in g ∫ phi psibar psi. In the weight written with a picture they are absorbed into the vertices, each of which stands for minus its coupling: lambda^n in the coefficient of a term becomes (-1)^n, so that the tadpole -lambda/2 G(a, z) G(z, z) G(z, b) has the weight 1/2. The expressions are not changed.

nodes.name: DeclareDisplayName
nodes.usage: DeclareDisplayName[h, name] displays h[x, y, ...] as name with the subscript x y ..., for example DeclareDisplayName[BareGreenFunction, "G0"]: input keeps the explicit name, output is compact.

nodes.name: DeclareLocalVertex
nodes.usage: DeclareLocalVertex[h, ...] declares heads of local vertices: kernels such as the quark-gluon vertex h[x, y, z] or the three-gluon vertex, whose labels carry different indices (Lorentz, colour, spinor) at one point of space-time. The pictures draw h[x, y, ...] as one point, at which its lines meet, instead of a grey blob; in the weight written with a picture the vertex stands for minus its kernel, -h (the sign of exp(-S_int)).

nodes.name: DeclareBlob
nodes.usage: DeclareBlob[h, label] draws a factor h[x1, ..., xn] (n >= 2, a self-energy h[x, y] included) as a blob with label (a LaTeX string, e.g. "\\Sigma") written inside; its legs leave it counterclockwise from the top left, at the corners of a square for n = 4, and its lines leave from these corners, as from those of a triangle (a point that is twice an argument, h[z, z, w, w], stands outside two corners, joined to each). Options: "Shape" -> "Circle" (default), "Box" or "Triangle" (equilateral, three legs at its corners, two on the left and one on the right: the vertex of a one-body operator), or "TriangleUp" (the same triangle with two legs at the bottom and one at the top), "Diamond" (a square turned by 45 degrees, legs at the left, bottom, right and top corners); "AxialPorts" -> {k1, ...}: the lines and legs of these ports leave horizontally, so that a self-energy can be drawn with its fermion line on an axis (the default for "TriangleUp" is {1, 2}); "Fill" -> "Hatched" (default), "CrossHatched", "Grey" or "White". A blob is as large as its label needs: the label (on a hatched blob in a white clearing, with a band of hatching left around it) sits at the centre, or near the incentre of a triangle, and a label with an accent, a subscript or a superscript makes the blob a little larger, never the label smaller; in one picture, and in all the terms of a sum drawn together, the blobs of one shape have one size. Blobs joined by lines are drawn side by side, as in the exact equations of many-body theory (Dyson, Schwinger-Dyson, Bethe-Salpeter, parquet).

nodes.name: ResetDeclarations
nodes.usage: ResetDeclarations[] removes all declarations (sources, fields, symmetries, derivative rules, line styles, interaction lines, couplings, local vertices, blobs, Matsubara frequencies): symmetric heads lose the attribute Orderless and antisymmetric ones their sign rules; display formats remain.

nodes.name: FunctionalDerivative
nodes.usage: FunctionalDerivative[F, s1, s2, ..., sn] is the functional (left) derivative δ/δs1 δ/δs2 ... δ/δsn F, the rightmost acting first. The si are sources, e.g. J[x] or eta[x], and must be declared. The result is in canonical form. FunctionalDerivative[F, {s1, ..., sn}] is the same. FunctionalDerivative[F, G[x, y]], with G a propagator or any other two-index kernel that is not a source (a self-energy, an interaction V, a background propagator), treats every G[a, b] as an independent variable (the derivative symmetrised for a symmetric G, DeclareSymmetric, and antisymmetrised, (δF/δG(x, y) - δF/δG(y, x))/2, for an antisymmetric one, DeclareAntisymmetric), as SelfEnergy does for the Luttinger-Ward functional: Σ(x, y) = δPhi/δG(y, x) and the irreducible vertex Γ0(x1, x2; x3, x4) = δ^2 Phi/δG(x4, x3) δG(x2, x1) (IrreducibleVertex) (fermions) are such derivatives. F may contain TraceLog, OperatorTrace, OperatorKernel and LegendreTransform (δ Tr ln A = Tr(A^-1 δA), δG^-1 = -G^-1 δG G^-1), and kernels whose dependence on a source is declared with DeclareFunctionalDerivative; an expression free of G gives 0 when G is a known kernel (a declared line, a symmetric head), the message nosource otherwise. A variation that is not known (a non-integer power of an operator) gives the message opvariation. FunctionalDerivative[F, s1, ..., sn, "MaximumOrder" -> {x, n}] is OrderPart[FunctionalDerivative[F, s1, ..., sn], x, Range[0, n]] for a coupling x or the head x of a line, with the terms of order above n dropped after each derivative; a logarithm of a sum polynomial in a coupling, such as Log[Z0 + Z1 + Z2/2], is first replaced by its series up to x^n (W = log Z order by order). When x is a source or a head with a declared derivative (the derivatives lower its order), the whole derivative is taken, then cut.

nodes.name: SimplifyDiagrams
nodes.usage: SimplifyDiagrams[expr] brings expr to canonical form: delta functions are integrated, integration variables are renamed canonically and equal diagrams are combined.

nodes.name: DiagramTerms
nodes.usage: DiagramTerms[expr] gives the list of the canonical terms (diagrams) of expr, each with its weight.

nodes.name: SetSourcesToZero
nodes.usage: SetSourcesToZero[expr] sets all declared sources to zero. It holds its argument: in SetSourcesToZero[FunctionalDerivative[F, s1, ..., sn]] the derivatives are taken one at a time, and after each the terms with more sources than derivatives left, which vanish at zero sources, are dropped; the result is the same as setting the sources to zero in the whole derivative.

nodes.name: FieldDerivative
nodes.usage: FieldDerivative[Z, {phi[x], psibar[y], ...}] applies to Z the source derivatives corresponding to the fields (see DeclareField), the rightmost first.

nodes.name: FieldExpectationValue
nodes.usage: FieldExpectationValue[Z, {fields...}] is the expectation value of the product of fields in the generating functional Z: the field derivatives of Z at zero sources divided by Z at zero sources. It is computed by literal differentiation.

nodes.name: GaussianExpectationValue
nodes.usage: GaussianExpectationValue[Z0, {fields...}] is the expectation value of a product of fields in a Gaussian generating functional Z0 (Wick's theorem). Option "Method" -> Automatic | "WickPairings" (sum over complete pairings, fast) | "Differentiation" (literal differentiation of Z0, which works for any Z0).

nodes.name: PerturbativeCorrelationFunction
nodes.usage: PerturbativeCorrelationFunction[Z0, {fields...}, interaction, n] is the expectation value <fields> = <fields exp(-interaction)>_0/<exp(-interaction)>_0 to order n in the interaction: all diagrams without vacuum bubbles. The interaction is written with the fields, e.g. lambda/24 IntegralOver[phi[z]^4, {z}]. With n = {k}, only order k; with {kmin, kmax}, orders kmin to kmax. Option "Method" -> Automatic | "WickPairings" | "Differentiation", as in GaussianExpectationValue; option "CouplingOrder" as in ConnectedCorrelationFunction.

nodes.name: ConnectedCorrelationFunction
nodes.usage: ConnectedCorrelationFunction[Z0, {fields...}, interaction, n] is the connected correlation function (cumulant) of the fields to order n: the diagrams in which all external points are connected, the derivatives of W = log Z with respect to the sources at zero source, computed order by order. Fields at the same point form a composite operator: the density-density function is ConnectedCorrelationFunction[Z0, {psibar[a], psi[a], psibar[b], psi[b]}, V, n], and psibar[a] ** psi[a] may stand for the two entries psibar[a], psi[a]; it is also -δG(a, a)/δU(b) for a potential U coupled to the density, whose derivative of the bare line is declared, DeclareFunctionalDerivative[G0[p_, q_], U[r_], G0[p, r] G0[r, q]]. With the option "CouplingOrder" -> {g, k} only the terms of order g^k are computed (the same as OrderPart[..., g, k], faster). Option "Method" as in PerturbativeCorrelationFunction.

nodes.name: ConnectedVacuumDiagrams
nodes.usage: ConnectedVacuumDiagrams[Z0, interaction, n] is log(Z/Z0) to order n in the interaction: the connected vacuum diagrams with their weights (linked-cluster theorem): the connected diagrams of Z/Z0 computed by derivatives (ConnectedDiagrams), directly. Options "Method" as in PerturbativeCorrelationFunction and "CouplingOrder" as in ConnectedCorrelationFunction.

nodes.name: OrderPart
nodes.usage: OrderPart[expr, x, k] keeps the terms of expr of order k: if x is a symbol (a coupling constant) the terms proportional to x^k; if x is the head of an interaction line, e.g. V, the terms with k factors V[...]. OrderPart[expr, x, {k1, k2, ...}] keeps the terms of the orders k1, k2, ....

nodes.name: ConnectedDiagrams
nodes.usage: ConnectedDiagrams[expr, {x1, ..., xn}] keeps the terms whose diagram is connected (the external labels x1, ..., xn and the integration variables are the points of the diagram).

nodes.name: DropVacuumBubbles
nodes.usage: DropVacuumBubbles[expr, {x1, ..., xn}] drops the terms containing vacuum bubbles, i.e. components without external points.

nodes.name: ParticleIrreducibleQ
nodes.usage: ParticleIrreducibleQ[term, n, {x1, ...}, {G, ...}] is True if the diagram of term stays connected after cutting any n or fewer lines with heads G, ... Interaction lines and vertices are never cut. External labels that end a single propagator are external legs (amputated before cutting); other external labels are vertices of the diagram.

nodes.name: ParticleIrreducibleDiagrams
nodes.usage: ParticleIrreducibleDiagrams[expr, n, {x1, ...}, {G, ...}] keeps the n-particle-irreducible terms of expr (see ParticleIrreducibleQ). With n = 1: one-particle irreducible (1PI) diagrams; with n = 2 and no external labels, ParticleIrreducibleDiagrams[vacuum, 2, {}, {G}]: the 2PI vacuum diagrams.

nodes.name: SkeletonDiagrams
nodes.usage: SkeletonDiagrams[expr, {x1, ..., xn}, {G, ...}] keeps the skeleton diagrams: one-particle irreducible and without self-energy insertions on the lines G. For a two-point function with external legs, these are the diagrams that close into 2PI vacuum diagrams; for amputated vertex functions, the diagrams in which no two lines G cut off a part without external labels.

nodes.name: ClosedLoopCount
nodes.usage: ClosedLoopCount[term, {G, ...}] is the number of closed loops made of the directed lines G (fermion loops) in the diagram of term.

nodes.name: DropClosedLoops
nodes.usage: DropClosedLoops[expr, {G, ...}] drops the terms with closed loops of the lines G, e.g. the fermion loops that cancel in a quenched average over disorder (replica limit).

nodes.name: AmputateExternalLegs
nodes.usage: AmputateExternalLegs[expr, {x1, ..., xn}, {G, ...}] removes the external legs: in every term, the propagator G that joins the external point xi to an internal vertex z is deleted and z is renamed xi (two external points ending on the same vertex give a DeltaFunction). Terms in which an external point is not joined to an internal vertex by a single propagator are dropped.

nodes.name: LuttingerWardFunctional
nodes.usage: LuttingerWardFunctional[Z0, interaction, n, G0 -> G] is the Luttinger-Ward functional to order n: minus the sum of the 2PI connected vacuum diagrams, with the bare propagator G0 replaced by the dressed one G. For bosons it is the 2PI part Γ2 of the effective action. LuttingerWardFunctional[Z0, interaction, n, {G0 -> G, D0 -> W, ...}] makes several propagators full at once: the diagrams that are 2PI with respect to all of them (e.g. the functional of G and of the screened interaction W of a Hubbard-Stratonovich field). Option "Method" as in PerturbativeCorrelationFunction.

nodes.name: SelfEnergy
nodes.usage: SelfEnergy[Phi, G, {x, y}] is the self-energy Σ(x, y) obtained from the Luttinger-Ward functional Phi: δPhi/δG(y, x) for fermions (option "Statistics" -> "Fermion", the default, with G = -<psi psibar>), -2 δPhi/δG(x, y) for real bosons ("Statistics" -> "Boson", with G = <phi phi> symmetric), -δPhi/δG(y, x) for complex bosons ("Statistics" -> "ComplexBoson", with G = <phi phibar>) and -2 δPhi/δG(x, y), the derivative antisymmetrised, for a superfield ("Statistics" -> "Superfield": a Grassmann field with an antisymmetric propagator G(a, b) = -<T NambuField_a NambuField_b>, e.g. the Nambu field NambuField = (psi, psibar), whose self-energy has the normal block Σ and the anomalous ones, the gap functions). In all cases G = G0 + G0 Σ G. It is a shortcut for the derivative: for fermions SelfEnergy[Phi, G, {x, y}] = FunctionalDerivative[Phi, G[y, x]], for real bosons -2 FunctionalDerivative[Phi, G[x, y]] (G symmetric: the derivative is symmetrised). On a symmetric or antisymmetric G without "Statistics" the fermionic default gives the message statisticsdefault.

nodes.name: IrreducibleVertex
nodes.usage: IrreducibleVertex[Phi, G, {x1, x2, x3, x4}] is the vertex irreducible in the particle-hole channel (x1 x2|x3 x4), the kernel of the Bethe-Salpeter equation: Γ0(x1, x2; x3, x4) = δΣ(x1, x2)/δG(x4, x3) = δ^2 Phi/δG(x4, x3) δG(x2, x1) for fermions (fermions leave at x1, x3 and enter at x2, x4), -2 δΣ(x1, x2)/δG(x3, x4) for real bosons, δΣ(x1, x2)/δG(x4, x3) for complex bosons ("Statistics" -> "ComplexBoson"), and -2 δΣ(a, b)/δG(c, d) = 4 δ^2 Phi/δG(a, b) δG(c, d), antisymmetrised, for a superfield ("Statistics" -> "Superfield"), the kernel of the channel s (a b|c d). Option "Channel": the kernel irreducible in another channel, from the same functional: for real bosons and superfields "s" (the default), "t" (a c|b d), "u" (a d|b c) or All (an association), Γ_t(a, b, c, d) = ±Γ_s(a, c, b, d) and Γ_u(a, b, c, d) = Γ_s(a, d, b, c), with the sign + for real bosons and - for superfields (the sign of the permutation); each is F - R_r (ParquetDecomposition). For fermions "ParticleHole" (the default) and "TransverseParticleHole", -Γ0(x3, x2; x1, x4); the particle-particle kernel is a derivative with respect to the anomalous propagators -<T psi psi>, -<T psibar psibar>: it is the channel t of the superfield (psi, psibar) projected with SuperfieldComponents, and "ParticleParticle" gives the message ppkernel. As a derivative of the components of the superfield Phi[G, Gpsipsi, Gpsibarpsibar] (SuperfieldComponents), Γ_pp(x1, x2; x3, x4) = -4 δ^2 Phi/δGpsipsi(x2, x4) δGpsibarpsibar(x1, x3) at zero anomalous propagators, i.e. -4 FunctionalDerivative[Phi, Gpsipsi[x2, x4], Gpsibarpsibar[x1, x3]] with Gpsipsi, Gpsibarpsibar then set to 0. IrreducibleVertex is a shortcut for the derivatives: for fermions IrreducibleVertex[Phi, G, {x1, x2, x3, x4}] = FunctionalDerivative[Phi, G[x4, x3], G[x2, x1]], for real bosons 4 FunctionalDerivative[Phi, G[x3, x4], G[x1, x2]].

nodes.name: PerturbativeFullVertex
nodes.usage: PerturbativeFullVertex[Z0, interaction, n, fields, {x1, x2, x3, x4}, G0 -> G] is the full (amputated, one-particle irreducible) four-point vertex F to order n, as a skeleton expansion in the dressed propagator G. For fermions, fields = {psi, psibar} and <psi(x1') psibar(x2') psibar(x4') psi(x3')>_c = G(x1', x1) G(x2, x2') F(x1, x2; x3, x4) G(x4, x4') G(x3', x3); for real bosons, fields = {phi} and F is the 1PI vertex Γ^(4) = -(amputated connected four-point function), and so for a superfield (one Grassmann field with an antisymmetric propagator, fields = {NambuField}). The order n can be n, {k} or {kmin, kmax}; option "Method" as in PerturbativeCorrelationFunction. Several bare propagators made full at once are a list of rules, {G0up -> Gup, G0down -> Gdown}. It is ConnectedCorrelationFunction[Z0, {psi[x1], psibar[x2], psibar[x4], psi[x3]}, interaction, n] amputated (AmputateExternalLegs) with its skeleton diagrams kept (SkeletonDiagrams) and G0 -> G; with spin, fields that carry the index of their sources (psi[x1, up], ...) are written in this way, the fields psi[x] without it giving the message fieldarity. With bare lines, F is ParticleIrreducibleDiagrams[AmputateExternalLegs[...], 1, ...] of the same function. The vertex is the fourth derivative of the 1PI action at zero means (EffectiveAction1PI with bare lines): the result is SkeletonDiagrams[SetSourcesToZero[FunctionalDerivative[Gamma, phiMean[x1], phiMean[x2], phiMean[x3], phiMean[x4]]], {x1, x2, x3, x4}, {G0}] /. G0 -> G, for fermions with the derivatives Psibar[x1], Psi[x2], Psibar[x3], Psi[x4]; this function computes the same from the connected function.

nodes.name: TwoParticleReducibleQ
nodes.usage: TwoParticleReducibleQ[term, {{x1, x2}, {x3, x4}}, {G, ...}] is True if cutting two or fewer lines G separates the external labels x1, x2 from x3, x4.

nodes.name: ReducibleDiagrams
nodes.usage: ReducibleDiagrams[expr, {{x1, ...}, {y1, ...}}, n, {G, ...}] keeps the terms in which cutting n or fewer lines G separates the external labels x1, ... from y1, ... For instance ReducibleDiagrams[chi, {{a}, {b}}, 1, {V}] keeps the diagrams of a response function that fall apart when a single interaction line is cut (the RPA-reducible ones).

nodes.name: IrreducibleDiagrams
nodes.usage: IrreducibleDiagrams[expr, {{x1, ...}, {y1, ...}}, n, {G, ...}] keeps the terms in which no cut of n or fewer lines G separates the external labels x1, ... from y1, ..., e.g. the proper polarisation IrreducibleDiagrams[chi, {{a}, {b}}, 1, {V}].

nodes.name: ParquetDecomposition
nodes.usage: ParquetDecomposition[F, {x1, x2, x3, x4}, {G, ...}] classifies the diagrams of a four-point vertex by two-particle reducibility and returns an association with the fully irreducible part "FullyIrreducible" and the reducible parts of the three channels: for fermions ("Statistics" -> "Fermion", legs x1, x3 outgoing and x2, x4 incoming) "ParticleHole" (x1 x2|x3 x4), "TransverseParticleHole" (x1 x4|x3 x2) and "ParticleParticle" (x1 x3|x2 x4); for real bosons and superfields ("Statistics" -> "Boson" or "Superfield") "s" (x1 x2|x3 x4), "t" (x1 x3|x2 x4) and "u" (x1 x4|x2 x3). Diagrams reducible in more than one channel, which the parquet theorem excludes, are collected under "SeveralChannels". The parts found by cutting lines are derivatives, which the classification checks: "FullyIrreducible" is the fourth derivative of the 2PI action with respect to the means at fixed G (EffectiveAction2PI with "MeanFields"), and F minus the part reducible in a channel is the kernel of that channel, a second derivative of Phi (IrreducibleVertex).

nodes.name: BetheSalpeterLadder
nodes.usage: BetheSalpeterLadder[L, R, {x1, x2, x3, x4}, channel, G] is the contraction L ∘ R of two four-point vertices with a pair of propagators G in the given channel, integrated over the internal points 5, 6, 7, 8. Fermions (legs x1, x3 outgoing, x2, x4 incoming; G(a, b) runs from b to a): "ParticleHole": L(x1, x2; 5, 6) G(6, 7) G(8, 5) R(7, 8; x3, x4); "TransverseParticleHole": -L(x1, 6; 5, x4) G(6, 7) G(8, 5) R(7, x2; x3, 8); "ParticleParticle": -1/2 L(x1, 5; x3, 6) G(5, 7) G(6, 8) R(7, x2; 8, x4). Real bosons ("Statistics" -> "Boson"): "s", "t", "u", e.g. -1/2 L(x1, x2, 5, 6) G(5, 7) G(6, 8) R(7, 8, x3, x4); superfields ("Statistics" -> "Superfield", G antisymmetric): the same with the signs +1/2, -1/2, +1/2 in s, t, u. With these conventions every channel obeys R_r = Γ_r ∘ F (Bethe-Salpeter) and F = Γirr + Sum_r R_r (parquet, Γirr the fully irreducible vertex). Option "MaximumOrder" -> {V, n} keeps only the products of order n or less.

nodes.name: CheckParquetEquations
nodes.usage: CheckParquetEquations[F, {x1, x2, x3, x4}, G, coupling, n] checks, order by order up to n, that every diagram of the vertex F is reducible in at most one channel and that the reducible part of each channel equals the Bethe-Salpeter ladder Γ_r ∘ F, with Γ_r = F - R_r. It returns an association with the residuals (all 0 if the equations hold) and the number of diagrams per order and channel. Option "Statistics": "Fermion" (the default), "Boson" or "Superfield", for the channels and the ladders of BetheSalpeterLadder.

nodes.name: PerturbativeDensityVertex
nodes.usage: PerturbativeDensityVertex[Z0, V, n, {psi, psibar}, {x1, x2, z}, G0 -> G] is the vertex of the density at z, Λ(x1, x2; z) = -δG^-1(x1, x2)/δU(z) for a potential U coupled to ρ = psibar psi: <psi(x1) psibar(x2) ρ(z)>_c = L0 Λ, with L0 the pair of propagators G(x1, a) G(b, x2) (integrated over a, b). It is δ(x1, z) δ(x2, z) plus the skeleton diagrams to order n, with the bare propagator G0 replaced by G. For a real boson field, PerturbativeDensityVertex[Z0, V, n, {phi}, {x1, x2, z}, D0 -> G] is the vertex of ρ = phi^2/2 (a local mass term). It is the derivative Λ = δ(x1, z) δ(x2, z) + δΣ(x1, x2)/δU(z) of the perturbative self-energy through its bare lines (DeclareFunctionalDerivative[G0[p_, q_], U[r_], G0[p, r] G0[r, q]]; for a real boson δ(x1, z) δ(x2, z) - δΣ/δU with δD0(p, q)/δU(r) = -D0(p, r) D0(r, q)), its skeleton diagrams with G0 -> G; this function computes the same from <psi psibar ρ>_c. Option "Method" as in PerturbativeCorrelationFunction.

nodes.name: LabelFunction
nodes.usage: LabelFunction[e, {x1, ..., xn}] is the function of n labels that gives e with x1, ..., xn replaced by its arguments: a perturbative series used as an object of ExactEquation.

nodes.name: ExactEquation
nodes.usage: ExactEquation[name, {"G" -> G, "Sigma" -> S, ...}, labels] is an exact equation between full objects, lhs == rhs. The objects are heads (e.g. blobs declared by DeclareBlob, to draw the equation) or functions of their labels (LabelFunction of perturbative series, to check it with CheckEquation). Fermions leave a four-point vertex at x1, x3 and enter at x2, x4. Names and objects: "Dyson" (G, G0, Sigma; labels {x, y}): G = G0 + G0 Σ G. "BetheSalpeter" (F, Gamma0, G; {x1, x2, x3, x4}; option "Channel"): F = Γ0 + Γ0 o F. "Parquet" (F, Lambda, GammaPh, GammaPhbar, GammaPp, G; for bosons Gammas, Gammat, Gammau): F = Γirr + Sum_r Γ_r o F, with the fully irreducible vertex Γirr (the object Lambda). "SchwingerDyson" (Sigma, G, F, V; {x, y}): Σ = Hartree + Fock - V G L0 F for a density-density interaction V; for real bosons (Sigma, G, F, Coupling) Σ = -λ/2 G(x, x) + λ/6 G L0 F in ϕ^4 theory. "Vertex" (Lambda, Gamma0, G; {x1, x2, z}): Λ = γ + Γ0 L0 Λ for the vertex of the density (L0 the pair of propagators of the channel), γ = δ(x1, z) δ(x2, z). "VertexFromF" (Lambda, F, G): Λ = γ + F L0 γ. "SelfEnergyFromVertex" (Sigma, G, V, Lambda; {x, y}): Σ = Hartree - V G Λ. "Hedin" (Sigma, G, W, P, Lambda, GammaXC, V; {x, y, z}): Hedin's equations Σ = Hartree - G W Λ, P = L0 Λ, W = V + V P W, Λ = γ + Γxc L0 Λ, with the proper vertex Λ and Γxc = δΣxc/δG. Option "Statistics" -> "Boson" for real bosons (BetheSalpeter, Parquet, SchwingerDyson, Vertex, VertexFromF). Option "MaximumOrder" -> {x, n}: both sides only up to order n in x, enough for CheckEquation to order n (the products of two series are not brought into canonical form beyond it). "Response" (L, Gamma0, G; {x1, x2, x3, x4}): L = L0 + L0 Γ0 L, the Bethe-Salpeter equation of the response of G to a one-body source, with L0 the pair of propagators; fermions (the legs of a four-point vertex: leaving at x1, x3, entering at x2, x4) L(x1, x2; x3, x4) = δG(x1, x2)/δU(x4, x3) = -<psi(x1) psibar(x2) psi(x3) psibar(x4)>_c + G(x1, x4) G(x3, x2), L = G(x1, x4) G(x3, x2) + G(x1, a) G(b, x2) Γ0(a, b; c, d) L(d, c; x3, x4); real bosons L = -2 δG/δU = <phi phi phi phi>_c + G13 G24 + G14 G23, L(x1, x2; x3, x4) = G(x1, x3) G(x2, x4) + G(x1, x4) G(x2, x3) - 1/2 G(x1, a) G(x2, b) Γ0(a, b; c, d) L(c, d; x3, x4). "Susceptibility" (Chi, L, optionally BareVertex; {z1, z2}): χ = γ L γ, the response δ<O(z1)>/δu(z2) = δ^2 Ω/δu δu = -<O O>_c of O(z) = ∫ psibar(a) γ(a, b; z) psi(b) (1/2 phi γ phi for real bosons, with a factor -1/4), the density when no "BareVertex" -> gamma (a function of three labels: current, spin, ...) is given. "Vertex" and "VertexFromF" also take "BareVertex" -> gamma, for the vertex of a general one-body operator.

nodes.name: CheckEquation
nodes.usage: CheckEquation[lhs == rhs, x, n] is the list of the residuals SimplifyDiagrams[lhs - rhs] of orders 0, ..., n in x: all 0 if the equation holds to order n. CheckEquation[{eq1, eq2, ...}, x, n] checks several equations.

nodes.name: HubbardStratonovich
nodes.usage: HubbardStratonovich[{Z0, interaction}, O, {phi, J}, D] decouples an interaction 1/2 Integral K(x, y) O(x) O(y), with O a local operator given as a function of one label (psibar[#] ** psi[#] &, or phi[#]^2 &), by a real auxiliary field phi with source J: <phi phi>_0 = K and the coupling -i Integral phi O, since <exp(i Integral phi O)> = exp(-1/2 Integral O K O). The kernel K is read off the interaction (two-label terms, or local terms like lambda/4! phi^4). D is the head of the propagator of phi, standing for K; with D = Automatic and K = c h[x, y], the head h itself is the propagator and Sqrt[c] goes into the coupling. The result is an association: "FreeGeneratingFunctional" (Z0 times the Gaussian of phi), "Interaction", "Propagator" and "Kernel" (K as a function of two labels, to substitute D back). The field and the source are declared, and the propagator of the field declared symmetric and, if it has no line style yet, an interaction line.

nodes.name: IntegrateOutField
nodes.usage: IntegrateOutField[{Z0, interaction}, phi, J] integrates out a real Gaussian field phi with source J, <phi phi>_0 = D (read off Z0), that enters the interaction linearly, Integral phi(z) A(z): since <exp(-Integral phi A)> = exp(1/2 Integral A D A), the interaction becomes the other terms - 1/2 Integral A(x) D(x, y) A(y). The result is an association with the "FreeGeneratingFunctional" without phi and the "Interaction". The converse of HubbardStratonovich; for phonons it gives the effective retarded interaction of the electrons.

nodes.name: DysonSeries
nodes.usage: DysonSeries[sigma, {s1, s2}, G0, {x, y}, m] is G0(x, y) + G0 Σ G0 + G0 Σ G0 Σ G0 + ... with up to m self-energy insertions, where sigma is an expression for Σ(s1, s2). With the option "MaximumOrder" -> {V, n}, only the chains of total order n or less in V (a coupling symbol or the head of the interaction lines) are built.

nodes.name: ConnectedFunctionFromVertices
nodes.usage: ConnectedFunctionFromVertices[{x1, ..., xn}, "Boson" | "Fermion"] gives the connected n-point function at zero source as a sum of trees of full propagators FullPropagator and one-particle-irreducible vertices VertexFunction (the tree expansion), obtained by differentiating the full propagator with respect to the source ExternalSource with the rules that follow from the Legendre transform. ConnectedFunctionFromVertices[n, type] uses the labels x1, ..., xn; the type is "Boson" by default. "Fermion" gives the trees of a superfield (psi, psibar), with antisymmetric propagator and vertices; "FermionLines" gives them with fermion lines: <psi(x1) psibar(x2) psi(x3) psibar(x4) ...>_c as trees of directed propagators FullPropagator[x, y] = G(x, y) = -<psi(x) psibar(y)>_c and vertices VertexFunction[outs..., ins...], antisymmetric within the outgoing and within the incoming legs; ConnectedFunctionFromVertices[labels, "FermionLines", {"Out" | "In", ...}] chooses psi ("Out") or psibar ("In") for each label.

nodes.name: FullPropagator
nodes.usage: FullPropagator[x, y] is the full (dressed) propagator G, the connected two-point function at the current source, used by ConnectedFunctionFromVertices.

nodes.name: VertexFunction
nodes.usage: VertexFunction[x1, ..., xn] is the one-particle-irreducible vertex Γ^(n), used by ConnectedFunctionFromVertices.

nodes.name: MeanField
nodes.usage: MeanField[x] is the mean field <phi(x)> at the current source, displayed as phi with a bar (the expectation value of the field, the exact one-point function, not a mean-field approximation), used by ConnectedFunctionFromVertices.

nodes.name: ExternalSource
nodes.usage: ExternalSource[x] is the source J(x) with respect to which ConnectedFunctionFromVertices differentiates.

nodes.name: DrawDiagram
nodes.usage: DrawDiagram[term, {x1, ..., xn}, options] draws one term as a Feynman diagram. Propagators are lines, interaction lines are wavy (see DeclareLineStyle), factors with three or more labels are grey blobs (vertex functions), factors with one label are source insertions. External points of correlation functions are open circles; in amputated vertex functions (self-energies, vertices) the external labels sit on vertices and are drawn as external legs; labels joined by a DeltaFunction are the same point. Options as for DiagramPlot.

nodes.name: DiagramPlot
nodes.usage: DiagramPlot[expr, {x1, ..., xn}, options] draws every canonical term of expr with its weight: the number written in front of a picture, times the values of its elements, is the term. A propagator stands for itself, an interaction line (DeclareInteractionLine) for minus its kernel, a local vertex (DeclareLocalVertex) for minus its kernel, and a vertex for minus its coupling (DeclareCoupling): the minus signs come from expanding exp(-S_int). An anomalous line ("DivergingArrows", "ConvergingArrows") or an antisymmetric blob of two labels shows no orientation: the weight takes it read along its fermion line, around a loop in either sense, along an open line from its end at the first external label. A kernel OperatorKernel[D^-1] is drawn as a line: in a term with lines D (a derivative of a trace before ExpandTrace) it gives the message inversekernel. Options: "VertexLabels" -> Automatic (external labels) | All (also z1, z2, ...) | None; "LegDirections" -> Automatic | "Alternating" | {"Out", "In", ...} (arrows on the external legs of fermionic vertex functions); "AmputatedLegs" -> Automatic | True | False; "InteractionStyle" -> Automatic | "Wavy" | "DoubleWavy" | "Curly" | "Dashed" | "Dotted" | "Zigzag" (the style of all the interaction lines); "Directed" -> {G, ...} and "Interactions" -> {V, ...} (heads drawn as arrows or as interaction lines in this picture only); "Couplings" -> {g, ...} (couplings absorbed into the vertices in this picture only, as with DeclareCoupling); "ExternalOrder" -> Automatic | {x1, ...}; "Columns" -> n; "Weights" -> True | False | "Coefficients" (the coefficients of the terms, every line and vertex standing for its kernel); "LineWidth" -> width of the lines in points; "Output" -> "Grid" (a grid of weights and pictures); ImageSize -> width of the picture in pixels (Automatic: 46 pixels per diagram unit); "Appearance" -> Automatic (dark lines and text on a light notebook, light ones on a dark notebook, through LightDarkSwitched of Mathematica 14.3 or later; before 14.3 the light colours) | "Light" | "Dark" (forced, on a background of the paper colour: white, or the dark grey of a dark notebook; SetOptions[{DiagramPlot, DrawDiagram}, "Appearance" -> "Dark"] for a session). DiagramToTikZ ignores it: the TikZ code is for white pages.

nodes.name: DiagramToTikZ
nodes.usage: DiagramToTikZ[expr, {x1, ..., xn}, options] gives LaTeX/TikZ code for the diagrams of expr: a sum of tikzpictures with their weights, ready for a paper (it needs the TikZ library decorations.pathmorphing). Same options as DiagramPlot, plus "Scale" -> length of one diagram unit in cm (0.7), "LineWidth" -> width of the lines in pt (0.7; arrow heads, dashes and double lines follow), "LabelFont" -> LaTeX font command of the labels ("\\small"), "Labels" -> rules from labels to LaTeX strings, and "Output" -> "List" for a list of {weight, picture} strings.

nodes.name: ExpressionToLaTeX
nodes.usage: ExpressionToLaTeX[expr, options] gives the LaTeX code of a formula: integrals with their variables as a subscript, functions with their arguments in parentheses, delta functions, Grassmann products in their order. Options: "Names" -> {h -> "G_0", ...}, the LaTeX of heads and symbols (by default the name given with DeclareDisplayName, else the symbol name, with greek letters, trailing digits and a final bar recognised) and of subexpressions (FermiFunction[xi[p1]] -> "n_1"); "Labels" -> {x -> "x_1", ...}, the LaTeX of labels; "Subscripts" -> {xi, v, ...}, heads whose arguments are written as a subscript, xi[p] as \xi_{p} (dispersions and potentials in momentum space).

nodes.name: FermiFunction
nodes.usage: FermiFunction[e] is the Fermi function n_F(e) = 1/(e^(e/T) + 1) (inert; n_F(0) = 1/2). Its derivatives Derivative[k][FermiFunction][e] come from poles of higher order (self-energy insertions on a line).

nodes.name: BoseFunction
nodes.usage: BoseFunction[e] is the Bose function n_B(e) = 1/(e^(e/T) - 1) (inert).

nodes.name: DeclareMatsubaraFrequency
nodes.usage: DeclareMatsubaraFrequency[w, "Fermion"] or DeclareMatsubaraFrequency[{w1, w2, ...}, "Boson"] declares that the symbols are Matsubara frequencies of that statistics (ω_n = (2n + 1) π T, ν_n = 2n π T), written I w in expressions. Statistical factors at energies shifted by them are simplified by periodicity: n_F(e + I ν) = n_F(e), n_F(e + I ω) = -n_B(e), n_B(e + I ω) = -n_F(e).

nodes.name: MatsubaraSum
nodes.usage: MatsubaraSum[f, z, "Fermion"] is T Sum_n f(z = I ω_n) over the fermionic Matsubara frequencies, MatsubaraSum[f, z, "Boson"] the sum over the bosonic ones, for f rational in z with a denominator that factors into linear and quadratic factors (propagators), computed by residues: the sum over the poles of f of Res[f n_F] (fermions) or -Res[f n_B] (bosons); poles of order k give the derivatives of order k - 1 of n_F, n_B. Option "ConvergenceFactor" -> 1 (a factor e^(I ω_n 0+), as for a density), -1 (e^(-I ω_n 0+)) or 0 (symmetric sum, no factor): it matters only when f decays like 1/z, and with the default Automatic a message is given in that case and the symmetric sum is taken. For f = 1/(z - a) the three give n_F(a), n_F(a) - 1 and n_F(a) - 1/2 (fermions), -n_B(a), -n_B(a) - 1 and -n_B(a) - 1/2 (bosons). A summand that does not decay (the sum diverges) or that is not split into poles gives a message and $Failed. A summand may also contain logarithms, c Log[r] with r rational in z (the sums of Tr ln): T Sum_n e^(I η ω_n 0+) ln(a - I ω_n) = -Temperature Log[1 - FermiFunction[a]] + (1 - η)/2 a for fermions, -Temperature Log[1 + BoseFunction[a]] + (1 - η)/2 a for bosons (η = 1, -1, 0 the three convergence factors; -T ln(1 - n_F(a)) = T ln(1 + e^(-a/T))), each zero of r counting +1 and each pole -1, a constant factor nothing (the trace of the identity is zero); the factors of a real boson, ln(W^2 - z^2), give W - 2 Temperature Log[1 + BoseFunction[W]] with every ordering, the zero-point energy included.

nodes.name: LoopMomentum
nodes.usage: LoopMomentum[i] is the momentum of the i-th loop of a diagram evaluated by EvaluateMatsubara or DiagramLoopIntegral (unless the option "LoopMomenta" -> {p1, p2, ...} gives names); ExpressionToLaTeX writes it p_i, and ℓ_i in QED (in a MinkowskiLoopIntegral, and in Dirac and Lorentz objects outside one).

nodes.name: LoopFrequency
nodes.usage: LoopFrequency[i, statistics] is the Matsubara frequency of the i-th loop of a diagram (DiagramIntegrand), written I LoopFrequency[i, statistics] in the integrand.

nodes.name: MomentumSum
nodes.usage: MomentumSum[f, {p1, p2, ...}] is the inert integral over the loop momenta, ∫ d^dp1/(2π)^d ... f (or (1/V) Sum_p f).

nodes.name: DiagramIntegrand
nodes.usage: DiagramIntegrand[diagrams, {x1 -> {k1, I w1}, ...}, rules, options] routes momenta and Matsubara frequencies through each term of diagrams as EvaluateMatsubara does and gives, for each term, {"Weight" -> ..., "Integrand" -> ..., "LoopMomenta" -> ..., "LoopFrequencies" -> ..., "EqualTimeFrequency" -> ...}: the integrand before the frequency sums, a function of I LoopFrequency[i, statistics]; "EqualTimeFrequency" is the sum of the frequencies of the fermion lines at equal times, the exponent Ω of their convergence factor e^(I Ω 0+) for the default "ConvergenceFactor" -> 1 of EvaluateMatsubara (e^(-I Ω 0+) for -1, none for 0) (0 when there is none). Options as in EvaluateMatsubara: "SpinDegeneracy" (in the weight) and "LoopMomenta".

nodes.name: EvaluateMatsubara
nodes.usage: EvaluateMatsubara[diagrams, {x1 -> {k1, I w1}, x2 -> {k2, I w2}, ...}, rules] evaluates diagrams of the package (functions of labels: position, imaginary time, spin) in momentum and Matsubara frequency, for a translation-invariant system: ki and I wi enter the diagram at the external label xi (they add up to zero; the statistics of wi is declared by DeclareMatsubaraFrequency). The rules give the lines: head -> {"Fermion", xi} (G0(p, I ω) = 1/(I ω - xi[p]) for a line head[x, y] from y to x), head -> {"Instantaneous", v} (an even interaction v[q], instantaneous) or head -> {"Boson", Function[{q, z}, d]} (an even boson propagator, a rational function of z = I ν, e.g. 2 Ω[q]/(Ω[q]^2 - z^2) for the <ϕ ϕ> of the package). Each loop gives T Sum_n ∫ d^dp/(2π)^d: the frequency sums are done by MatsubaraSum, with the convergence factor e^(I ω 0+) of the lines at equal times (option "ConvergenceFactor"), and the momentum integrals are left as MomentumSum. A function of one external frequency is written in partial fractions of it (the denominators of the textbooks), separately in the parts of a term between the lines that carry that frequency alone (the external legs of a function that is not amputated, the lines between its irreducible parts), which stay as factors. Options: "SpinDegeneracy" -> 1 (a factor (2s + 1) for each closed fermion loop), "LoopMomenta" -> Automatic (LoopMomentum[i]) or a list of names, "ConvergenceFactor" -> 1 (the ordering of a fermion line at equal times, G[x, y] with x and y at the same time: 1 for e^(I ω 0+), G(τ = 0-) = <ψ^† ψ>, n_F(xi) for a line closed on itself; -1 for e^(-I ω 0+), G(0+) = -<ψ ψ^†>, n_F(xi) - 1; 0 for no factor, the symmetric sum, the mean (1/2) <[ψ^†, ψ]>, n_F(xi) - 1/2, natural on a lattice with a particle-hole symmetric interaction, where the difference is a shift of the chemical potential, but divergent in the continuum). Invalid arguments, or a term that cannot be evaluated, give a message and $Failed. Traces of operators are evaluated too (with no external point): TraceLog[A] and OperatorTrace[A], with A built from kernels that have line rules ("Fermion": 1/(z - xi[k]); "Instantaneous": v[k], e.g. a static self-energy; "Boson": f[k, z]), give (2s + 1) MomentumSum[T Sum_n e^(I η ω_n 0+) ln A(k, I ω_n)] and the same with A (its constant part dropped: Tr 1 = 0), per unit of β times the volume, as the vacuum diagrams: with EffectiveAction2PI this is the grand potential Ω/V, e.g. -Tr ln(-G0^-1) = 2 Temperature MomentumSum[Log[1 - FermiFunction[xi[p]]], {p}] for spin 1/2. Option "Limit" -> "Static" sets all external momenta and frequencies to zero (the limit q -> 0 at zero frequency, the thermodynamic response: at q = 0 the double poles give derivatives of n_F), "Dynamic" sets the external momenta to zero and takes the external frequency to zero at the end (zero for the density of a conserving approximation; a message if it diverges).

nodes.name: AnalyticContinuation
nodes.usage: AnalyticContinuation[expr, w -> omega] continues I w -> omega + I 0+ after the Matsubara sums (the retarded function): the result is a function of omega, understood as omega + I 0+. The statistical factors must be free of w (declare its statistics with DeclareMatsubaraFrequency before the sums).

nodes.name: RetardedImaginaryPart
nodes.usage: RetardedImaginaryPart[expr, omega] is the imaginary part of a retarded function of omega + I 0+ (the result of AnalyticContinuation) with real coefficients: 1/(omega - E + I 0+) -> -π EnergyDelta[omega - E], and poles of order k give derivatives of EnergyDelta. It works inside MomentumSum.

nodes.name: EnergyDelta
nodes.usage: EnergyDelta[x] is the inert delta function δ(x) of an energy; Derivative[k][EnergyDelta][x] are its derivatives.

nodes.name: CuttingRuleImaginaryPart
nodes.usage: CuttingRuleImaginaryPart[diagrams, externals, rules, w -> omega] is the imaginary part of a retarded two-point function from the cutting rules at finite temperature, computed in imaginary time without Matsubara sums: the cut separates the time vertex where I w enters from the one where it leaves, every cut line is on shell (EnergyDelta) with its factor of emission (1 - n_F, 1 + n_B) or absorption (n_F, n_B), and the factor 1 + e^(-omega/T) (fermions) or 1 - e^(-omega/T) (bosons) adds the inverse process. It is implemented for diagrams whose propagating lines form chains from one external time vertex to the other (bubbles, sunsets, with static insertions such as Hartree and Fock on the lines); other diagrams give CuttingRuleImaginaryPart::class and $Failed, and so does a frequency w that does not enter the diagram at one external point and leave it at another (CuttingRuleImaginaryPart::frequency). Arguments and options as in EvaluateMatsubara.

nodes.name: CheckCuttingRules
nodes.usage: CheckCuttingRules[diagrams, externals, rules, w -> omega] compares, term by term and for each EnergyDelta, the imaginary part of the retarded function from the Matsubara sums (EvaluateMatsubara, AnalyticContinuation, RetardedImaginaryPart) with the cutting rules (CuttingRuleImaginaryPart); statistical factors are compared through e^(e/T). It gives 0 if they agree, or the list of the differences ($Failed for a term to which the cutting rules do not apply), and $Failed for a frequency w that does not cross the diagram. Options as in EvaluateMatsubara.

nodes.name: ZeroTemperatureLimit
nodes.usage: ZeroTemperatureLimit[expr] is the limit T -> 0 of the statistical factors: n_F(e) -> UnitStep[-e], n_B(e) -> -UnitStep[-e], and their derivatives give derivatives of EnergyDelta (n_F'(e) -> -EnergyDelta[e]). n_F(0) = 1/2 at every temperature, while UnitStep[0] = 1: substitute an energy that may vanish before taking the limit. The terms of the sums of logarithms go as Temperature Log[1 - FermiFunction[e]] -> e UnitStep[-e] and Temperature Log[1 + BoseFunction[e]] -> 0.

nodes.name: Temperature
nodes.usage: Temperature is the temperature T of the statistical factors, n_F(e) = 1/(e^(e/Temperature) + 1) (FermiFunction) and n_B(e) = 1/(e^(e/Temperature) - 1) (BoseFunction). It appears explicitly only in the sums of logarithms of MatsubaraSum and in the traces Tr ln of EvaluateMatsubara: T Sum_n e^(I ω_n 0+) ln(a - I ω_n) = -Temperature Log[1 - FermiFunction[a]] = T ln(1 + e^(-a/T)), minus the grand potential of one level (Ω = -Tr ln(-G0^-1) per level).

nodes.name: ScalarPropagator
nodes.usage: ScalarPropagator[q, m] is the Euclidean scalar propagator 1/(q^2 + m^2) of a line with momentum q (a linear combination of momenta) and mass m (0 for a massless line); ScalarPropagator[q, m]^a is 1/(q^2 + m^2)^a, with a any power (massless lines get powers a + b - 2 + ϵ from the one-loop integrals inside them).

nodes.name: MomentumSquared
nodes.usage: MomentumSquared[q] is the square q^2 of a momentum q, a linear combination of momenta (c p gives c^2 p^2 for a single momentum p and a number c).

nodes.name: RenormalizationScale
nodes.usage: RenormalizationScale is the scale μ of dimensional regularization: every loop is μ^(2ϵ) (e^γE/(4π))^ϵ ∫ d^dk/(2π)^d, d = 4 - 2ϵ (the MS-bar measure: minimal subtraction of the poles in ϵ is then the MS-bar scheme, and μ is the MS-bar scale).

nodes.name: LoopIntegral
nodes.usage: LoopIntegral[f, {k1, k2, ...}] is the inert Euclidean loop integral of f over the loop momenta k1, k2, ..., each with the MS-bar measure μ^(2ϵ) (e^γE/(4π))^ϵ ∫ d^dk/(2π)^d in d = 4 - 2ϵ (μ = RenormalizationScale); f is a product of ScalarPropagator factors, possibly with numerators that are squares of momenta (MomentumSquared[q], or k^2 for a loop momentum k). It depends on ϵ only through d: EpsilonExpand refuses it (evaluate it first with IntegrateLoops).

nodes.name: DiagramLoopIntegral
nodes.usage: DiagramLoopIntegral[diagrams, {x1 -> p1, x2 -> p2, ...}, {G0 -> {"Scalar", m}, ...}] is the momentum-space form of the diagrams of the package (functions of labels, local vertices), for a translation-invariant theory at zero temperature in Euclidean space: the momentum pi enters at the external label xi (they add up to zero), the momenta are routed through the lines as in EvaluateMatsubara, and each term is its weight times LoopIntegral[product of the lines, loop momenta]. A rule G0 -> {"Scalar", m} makes the line G0[x, y] the propagator ScalarPropagator[q, m] = 1/(q^2 + m^2) (m = 0: massless); G0 -> {"Kernel", f} gives it the value f[q] (an insertion such as a counterterm). The momentum q of a line is written with the sign that makes its first term positive, so f must be even, f[-q] = f[q] (a function of q^2). Option "LoopMomenta" -> {k1, ...} names the loop momenta (default LoopMomentum[i]).

nodes.name: IntegrateLoops
nodes.usage: IntegrateLoops[expr, ϵ] evaluates the LoopIntegral objects of expr in d = 4 - 2ϵ when the loops can be done one after the other as one-loop integrals: at each step a loop momentum that appears in at most two different propagators is integrated, giving a tadpole (TadpoleIntegral), a massless one-loop integral (GFunction times (P^2)^(2 - ϵ - a - b), a new massless line of non-integer power) or a massive bubble (BubbleIntegral). This covers the massless propagator-type integrals that reduce to nested one-loop ones (the sunset, bubble insertions, the two-loop four-point diagrams with the external momentum through two legs) and products of massive one-loop factors. Numerators q^2 are written 1/ScalarPropagator[q, m] - m^2 with the mass of a line of the same momentum (1/ScalarPropagator[q, 0] otherwise); a numerator in a bubble with a massive line is reduced to tadpoles. Scaleless integrals are 0, as in dimensional regularization; when one of them is logarithmically divergent, its ultraviolet pole (cancelled by an infrared one) is lost, and a message says so. A message is also given for an infrared divergence (a massless line of power 2 or more at ϵ = 0, or of zero momentum): the poles of the result are then not only ultraviolet ones. For ultraviolet counterterms give the lines a mass, or use InfraredRearrangedIntegral. A loop integral that is not reduced gives a message and stays unevaluated.

nodes.name: GFunction
nodes.usage: GFunction[a, b, ϵ] is the coefficient G(a, b) = Γ(d/2 - a) Γ(d/2 - b) Γ(a + b - d/2)/(Γ(a) Γ(b) Γ(d - a - b)), d = 4 - 2ϵ, of the massless one-loop integral ∫ d^dk/(2π)^d 1/((k^2)^a ((k + p)^2)^b) = (4π)^(-d/2) G(a, b) (p^2)^(d/2 - a - b); a and b can be any powers.

nodes.name: TadpoleIntegral
nodes.usage: TadpoleIntegral[a, m, ϵ] is the one-loop tadpole ∫_k 1/(k^2 + m^2)^a with the MS-bar measure of LoopIntegral: e^(ϵ γE) μ^(2ϵ) Γ(a - d/2)/(16 π^2 Γ(a)) (m^2)^(d/2 - a), exact in d = 4 - 2ϵ (0 for m = 0, and for a power a that is an integer a <= 0).

nodes.name: BubbleIntegral
nodes.usage: BubbleIntegral[{a, b}, p2, {m1, m2}, ϵ] is the one-loop bubble ∫_k 1/((k^2 + m1^2)^a ((k + p)^2 + m2^2)^b) at p^2 = p2, with the MS-bar measure of LoopIntegral. It evaluates to closed forms in d when there is one: both lines massless (GFunction); a power that is an integer <= 0 (a numerator, reduced to tadpoles); p2 = 0 with equal masses or a massless line (tadpoles and Gamma functions) and p2 = 0 with unequal masses for a = b = 1 (partial fractions). Otherwise it stays as the Feynman-parameter integral e^(ϵ γE) μ^(2ϵ) Γ(a + b - d/2)/(16 π^2 Γ(a) Γ(b)) ∫_0^1 dx x^(a - 1) (1 - x)^(b - 1) Δ^(d/2 - a - b), Δ = x (1 - x) p2 + x m1^2 + (1 - x) m2^2, which EpsilonExpand expands when the powers are positive, independent of ϵ, and less than 2 on a massless line: in closed form (logarithms; the square root of the Källén function, and ArcTanh for equal masses) for the finite part of a = b = 1 and for a + b = 3, as FeynmanParameterIntegral beyond.

nodes.name: FeynmanParameterIntegral
nodes.usage: FeynmanParameterIntegral[f, FeynmanParameter] is the inert integral ∫_0^1 dx f of the Feynman parameter x = FeynmanParameter, left by EpsilonExpand for the coefficients of a massive bubble that it does not give in closed form; N evaluates it by NIntegrate (N[expr, n] to n digits).

nodes.name: FeynmanParameter
nodes.usage: FeynmanParameter is the Feynman parameter x, integrated from 0 to 1, in FeynmanParameterIntegral[f, FeynmanParameter]. FeynmanParameter[i] are the Feynman parameters of IntegrateOneLoop (in ParameterIntegral and SimplexIntegral).

nodes.name: EpsilonExpand
nodes.usage: EpsilonExpand[expr, ϵ, n] is the Laurent expansion of expr in ϵ up to ϵ^n included, computed without Series: Gamma functions of arguments n0 + c ϵ through PolyGamma (and their recurrence at the poles), powers X^(c ϵ) through logarithms (ln(X/μ^2) when the powers of μ = RenormalizationScale balance them), exponentials and rational functions of ϵ term by term, and massive bubbles (BubbleIntegral in this ϵ) through their Feynman parameters. With the MS-bar measure of LoopIntegral no Euler constant and no ln(4π) appears. An unevaluated LoopIntegral or MinkowskiLoopIntegral, whose dependence on ϵ is not explicit, gives a message and $Failed.

nodes.name: PolePart
nodes.usage: PolePart[expr, ϵ] is the part of the Laurent expansion of expr with negative powers of ϵ (EpsilonExpand[expr, ϵ, -1]): the MS-bar counterterm is minus it.

nodes.name: InfraredRearrangedIntegral
nodes.usage: InfraredRearrangedIntegral[diagrams, {x1, ..., xn}, p, rules, ϵ] evaluates each term of diagrams with one momentum p entering at one external label and leaving at another (the other external momenta zero), trying the pairs of labels in order until the term reduces to nested one-loop integrals without infrared divergences (no massless line of power 2 or more at ϵ = 0) and without logarithmically divergent scaleless integrals: the infrared rearrangement, legitimate for the ultraviolet poles of logarithmically divergent functions once their subdivergences are subtracted, since those are polynomial in the external momenta and the masses. A part of a term with a scaleless loop that is only power divergent in the ultraviolet (a massless tadpole) is 0: in a massless theory such a loop has no ultraviolet counterterm. A term without a valid routing gives a message and $Failed. Only the counterterms left after the subtraction of the subdivergences are physical: the finite parts and the pole parts of the single rearranged diagrams (with their logarithms of p^2/μ^2) depend on the routing. With the option "Routing" -> True the result is the list of {term, {label in, label out}, value}.

nodes.name: MassInsertion
nodes.usage: MassInsertion[diagrams, G0, z] is -∂/∂m^2 of the diagrams through their lines G0 = 1/(q^2 + m^2): the sum, over the lines G0[x, y], of the diagram with that line replaced by G0[x, z] G0[z, y], z a new external label, a symbol that does not appear in the diagrams (the insertion of the operator ϕ^2/2 at z). At m = 0 the momentum entering at z makes the infrared rearrangement of ∂Σ/∂m^2 possible (InfraredRearrangedIntegral).

nodes.name: BetaFunctionFromZ
nodes.usage: BetaFunctionFromZ[Z, g, ϵ, n] is the beta function β(g) = μ dg/dμ (at ϵ = 0, to order g^n) of a coupling renormalized as g_B = μ^(2ϵ) Z g (MS-bar, d = 4 - 2ϵ): β = -2 ϵ g/(1 + g ∂_g ln Z) + 2 ϵ g, expanded in g; the limit ϵ -> 0 must exist (a check of the poles of Z), otherwise a message is given. Option "ScalePower" -> s for g_B = μ^(s ϵ) Z g (s = 2 for λ ϕ^4, s = 1 for a gauge or Yukawa coupling in d = 4 - 2ϵ).

nodes.name: AnomalousDimensionFromZ
nodes.usage: AnomalousDimensionFromZ[Z, g, ϵ, betaEpsilon, n] is μ d ln Z/dμ = betaEpsilon ∂_g ln Z at ϵ = 0, to order g^n, with betaEpsilon = -s ϵ g + β(g) the beta function in d = 4 - 2ϵ (s = 2 for g_B = μ^(2ϵ) Z_g g); the limit ϵ -> 0 must exist, otherwise a message is given. For a field ϕ_B = Z_ϕ^(1/2) ϕ, γ_ϕ = 1/2 μ d ln Z_ϕ/dμ.

nodes.name: GammaMatrix
nodes.usage: GammaMatrix[μ] is the Dirac matrix γ^μ in d dimensions (Minkowski metric (+,-,-,-), {γ^μ, γ^ν} = 2 g^μν, Tr 1 = 4). The Lorentz indices are abstract: an index that appears twice in a term is contracted, more than twice is an error, and explicit components (GammaMatrix[0], ...) are not supported. There is no γ5: GammaMatrix[5] is refused by DiracSimplify, DiracOrder and IntegrateOneLoop (message GammaMatrix::gamma5; $Failed, or the integral left unevaluated).

nodes.name: SlashedMomentum
nodes.usage: SlashedMomentum[p] is p-slash = γ^μ p_μ, linear in p: a linear combination of momenta (symbols, or objects such as p[1] and LoopMomentum[i]) with coefficients that are numbers or polynomials in FeynmanParameter[i]. A symbolic coefficient (x p, m p, p/m) is ambiguous: the object is left as it is, with the message DiracSimplify::momentum.

nodes.name: DiracProduct
nodes.usage: DiracProduct[a, b, ...] is the product of Dirac matrices a b ... (GammaMatrix, SlashedMomentum, sums of them and scalars); DiracProduct[] is the unit matrix. DiracSimplify expands it, takes the scalars out and contracts its indices. A product of matrices written with Times or Power is refused (DiracSimplify::product).

nodes.name: DiracTrace
nodes.usage: DiracTrace[X] is the trace of the Dirac matrix X (Tr 1 = 4, no γ5); DiracSimplify evaluates it.

nodes.name: SpinorChain
nodes.usage: SpinorChain[{p2, m2}, X, {p1, m1}] is ubar(p2) X u(p1), with on-shell spinors: p2^2 = m2^2, p1^2 = m1^2, ubar(p2) p2-slash = m2 ubar(p2), p1-slash u(p1) = m1 u(p1). DiracSimplify moves p1-slash to the right and p2-slash to the left and uses the Dirac equation; the other momenta should be written in terms of p1 and p2 (q -> p2 - p1).

nodes.name: LorentzMetric
nodes.usage: LorentzMetric[μ, ν] is the metric g^μν (symmetric; g^μ_μ = d = SpacetimeDimension; abstract indices, no components).

nodes.name: FourVector
nodes.usage: FourVector[p, μ] is the component p^μ of the momentum p (μ an abstract index).

nodes.name: ScalarProduct
nodes.usage: ScalarProduct[p, q] is the Minkowski scalar product p·q (symmetric and bilinear; ScalarProduct[p, p] = p^2).

nodes.name: SpacetimeDimension
nodes.usage: SpacetimeDimension is the dimension d of the Dirac algebra (g^μ_μ = d); IntegrateOneLoop and ExpandParameterIntegrals set d = 4 - 2ϵ.

nodes.name: DiracSimplify
nodes.usage: DiracSimplify[expr] expands the Dirac matrices of expr (DiracProduct, DiracTrace, SpinorChain), makes slashed momenta, four-vectors and scalar products linear, contracts the repeated Lorentz indices (γ^μ γ_μ = d, γ^μ a γ_μ = (2 - d) a, γ^μ a b γ_μ = 4 a·b - (4 - d) a b, ..., in general γ^μ X a γ_μ = 2 a X - (γ^μ X γ_μ) a), p-slash p-slash = p^2, evaluates the traces and applies the Dirac equation in the spinor chains. It gives a message and $Failed for GammaMatrix[5], explicit component indices, a commutative product of matrices and an index that appears more than twice in a term (also in a term of the integrand of a loop integral); a momentum that is not a linear combination of momenta with coefficients that are numbers or polynomials in the Feynman parameters is left as it is (message). An unevaluated MinkowskiLoopIntegral is simplified inside (one in a SpinorChain or a DiracTrace is first taken out of it: the spinors do not depend on the loop momentum, which is renamed if a spinor has a momentum of the same name, and the trace is linear; an integrand that is 0 gives 0): its integrand is expanded and its indices are counted term by term, and in the term outside it counts with its free indices.

nodes.name: DiracOrder
nodes.usage: DiracOrder[expr] is DiracSimplify[expr] with the factors of every product put in a canonical order by {a, b} = 2 a·b: two expressions are equal when DiracOrder of their difference is 0.

nodes.name: QEDIntegrand
nodes.usage: QEDIntegrand[diagrams, {x1 -> p1, ...}, {S -> {"Fermion", m}, Ph -> {"Photon", ξ}, V -> {"Vertex", c}}] is the momentum-space form of one-loop diagrams of the package with spinor and Lorentz indices (condensed notation): S[x, y] = <T ψ(x) ψbar(y)> is the fermion line, i (q-slash + m)/(q^2 - m^2) with q flowing from y to x; Ph[z, w] the photon, -i [g^μν - (1 - ξ) q^μ q^ν/(q^2 - λ^2)]/(q^2 - λ^2) (Ph -> {"Photon", {ξ, λ}} for a photon mass λ, an infrared regulator); V[x, y, z] the local vertex c γ^μ (spinor indices of x and y, Lorentz index of z). The momentum pi enters at the external label xi (they add up to zero). The spinor indices are followed along the fermion lines: an open line is a DiracProduct (from its ψ end to its ψbar end), a closed loop a DiracTrace (its minus sign is in the weight of the package); at most one open line, one loop. Each term is its weight times MinkowskiLoopIntegral[numerator FeynmanDenominator[q, m]..., {k}]. Options "LoopMomentum" -> k (default LoopMomentum[1], written ℓ_1 by ExpressionToLaTeX) and "Indices" -> {x -> μ, ...} (the Lorentz index of a label; by default the label itself).

nodes.name: FeynmanDenominator
nodes.usage: FeynmanDenominator[q, m] is the Minkowski propagator denominator 1/(q^2 - m^2 + i0).

nodes.name: MinkowskiLoopIntegral
nodes.usage: MinkowskiLoopIntegral[f, {k}] is the inert one-loop integral of f over the loop momentum k with the measure μ^(2ϵ) (e^γE/(4π))^ϵ ∫ d^dk/(2π)^d in Minkowski space, d = 4 - 2ϵ (μ = RenormalizationScale; MS-bar); f is a product of FeynmanDenominator factors (integer powers; a negative power is a numerator) and of a numerator polynomial in k (slashed momenta, four-vectors, scalar products, Dirac products and traces). DiracSimplify simplifies its integrand, IntegrateOneLoop evaluates it.

nodes.name: IntegrateOneLoop
nodes.usage: IntegrateOneLoop[expr, ϵ] evaluates the MinkowskiLoopIntegral objects of expr in d = 4 - 2ϵ: Feynman parameters FeynmanParameter[i] for any number of denominators and any integer powers, the shift k = l - Σ xi ri, the tensor reduction l^μ1 ... l^μ2n -> (l^2)^n (sum of the products of metrics)/(d (d+2) ... (d+2n-2)) (odd ranks vanish), and ∫_l (l^2)^J/(l^2 - Δ)^A = i (-1)^(A+J) e^(ϵ γE) μ^(2ϵ) Γ(J + d/2) Γ(A - J - d/2)/(16 π^2 Γ(d/2) Γ(A)) Δ^(d/2 + J - A), with Δ - i0 (Feynman). The result is a sum of Dirac and tensor structures times exact Feynman-parameter integrals: ParameterIntegral (two denominators) or SimplexIntegral (three or more). An integral with more than one loop momentum, a non-integer power of a denominator or a numerator that is not polynomial in k is left unevaluated with a message; without a denominator depending on k it is 0 (scaleless).

nodes.name: SimplexIntegral
nodes.usage: SimplexIntegral[f, {x1, ..., xn}] is the inert Feynman-parameter integral ∫_0^1 dx1 ... dxn δ(1 - x1 - ... - xn) f. DifferentiateUnderIntegral differentiates under the integral sign, ReduceParameterIntegrals does it in closed form where possible, N evaluates it by NIntegrate over the unit cube, with Δ - i0: the logarithms and non-integer powers of a base that is negative somewhere (above a threshold) are Log|b| - iπ and |b|^a e^(-iπ a) there; N does not evaluate a power <= -1 of a base that changes sign in the region (with Δ - i0 the integral is finite, but NIntegrate cannot integrate the pole): SimplexIntegral::threshold and Indeterminate.

nodes.name: ParameterIntegral
nodes.usage: ParameterIntegral[f, x] is the inert integral ∫_0^1 dx f (exact in d: f may contain ϵ). DifferentiateUnderIntegral differentiates under the integral sign, ReduceParameterIntegrals does it in closed form where possible, N evaluates it by NIntegrate (N[expr, n] to n digits), with Δ - i0: the logarithms and non-integer powers of a base that is negative somewhere (above a threshold) are Log|b| - iπ and |b|^a e^(-iπ a) there, the interval split at the real roots of the bases; N does not evaluate a power <= -1 of a base with a root inside the interval (with Δ - i0 the integral is finite, but NIntegrate cannot integrate the pole): ParameterIntegral::threshold and Indeterminate.

nodes.name: ReduceParameterIntegrals
nodes.usage: ReduceParameterIntegrals[expr] does the Feynman-parameter integrals of expr where possible, exactly in d: a SimplexIntegral whose non-polynomial factors depend on one parameter only (after the delta function is used, e.g. the vertex at q^2 = 0), and polynomially on the others, is integrated over the others; a ParameterIntegral of powers of monomials c x^a (1 - x)^b, with exponents that do not depend on x (e.g. on shell), is a product of Gamma functions (infrared divergences then appear as poles in ϵ, dimensional regularization of the infrared). The powers c^a of the coefficients are taken at c - i0 when c is a negative number; for a symbolic c, c^a is the principal power (valid for c > 0, below thresholds). The others stay.

nodes.name: CombineParameterIntegrals
nodes.usage: CombineParameterIntegrals[expr] writes the Feynman-parameter integrals of expr that have the same variables and the same factor in front as one integral of the sum of their integrands. The factor in front is the Dirac or tensor structure and the factors that do not appear in the integrand, such as the coupling; the numbers and the other factors go into the integrand. ReduceParameterIntegrals does it at the end.

nodes.name: ExpandParameterIntegrals
nodes.usage: ExpandParameterIntegrals[expr, ϵ, n] is the Laurent expansion of expr in ϵ up to ϵ^n: ReduceParameterIntegrals, then EpsilonExpand, with the integrands of the remaining Feynman-parameter integrals expanded under the integral sign to the order that the factor in front of each needs (polynomial coefficients integrated exactly, the others inert ParameterIntegral and SimplexIntegral, evaluated by N). The expansion under the integral sign needs coefficients integrable at ϵ = 0: an integrand that is not (an infrared divergence at a face of the region, where a base vanishes) has its singular part subtracted, exactly in d (Beta functions times integrals over the face, which carry the infrared poles), when there is one singular face (in one dimension, each endpoint) and every factor of the singular terms that depends on the parameters is a power of a polynomial (as in the results of IntegrateOneLoop), the exponents of those that vanish there linear in ϵ and regulated by it; otherwise ExpandParameterIntegrals::ir and $Failed. Other factors (logarithms, Gamma functions of the parameters) are assumed regular and are not checked. A list is expanded element by element.

nodes.name: DifferentiateUnderIntegral
nodes.usage: DifferentiateUnderIntegral[expr, v] is the derivative of expr with respect to v, with the integrands of its ParameterIntegral and SimplexIntegral objects differentiated under the integral sign (e.g. d/dp^2 of a self-energy, for the wave-function renormalization).

nodes.name: VertexFormFactors
nodes.usage: VertexFormFactors[Γ, μ, {p1, p2, m}] gives {F1, F2, F3} for a vertex ubar(p2) Γ^μ u(p1) = ubar(p2) [γ^μ F1 + i σ^μν q_ν F2/(2m) + q^μ F3] u(p1), q = p2 - p1, between spinors of mass m (Γ a sum of SpinorChain[{p2, m}, ..., {p1, m}] terms; it is reduced by DiracSimplify to γ^μ A + p1^μ B1 + p2^μ B2 and decomposed by the Gordon identity: F1 = A + m (B1 + B2), F2 = -m (B1 + B2), F3 = (B2 - B1)/2). A part of another form gives VertexFormFactors::rest and $Failed.

nodes.name: EffectiveAction2PI
nodes.usage: EffectiveAction2PI[Phi, G0 -> G] is the two-particle-irreducible (2PI) effective action Γ[G] at zero mean field built on the Luttinger-Ward functional Phi (minus the 2PI vacuum diagrams, LuttingerWardFunctional): for fermions ("Statistics" -> "Fermion", the default, G = -<psi psibar>) Γ[G] = Phi[G] - Tr ln(-G^-1) - Tr(G0^-1 G - 1); for real bosons ("Boson", G = <phi phi> symmetric) Γ2[G] + 1/2 Tr ln G^-1 + 1/2 Tr(D0^-1 G - 1); for complex bosons ("ComplexBoson", G = <phi phibar>) Phi + Tr ln G^-1 + Tr(G0^-1 G - 1); for a superfield ("Superfield", a Grassmann field with the antisymmetric propagator G = -<T NambuField NambuField>, e.g. the Nambu field NambuField = (psi, psibar), whose propagator has the normal block and the anomalous ones -<T psi psi>, -<T psibar psibar>) Phi[G] - 1/2 Tr ln(-G^-1) - 1/2 Tr(G0^-1 G - 1), the Nambu-Gor'kov functional (the factor 1/2 of a Pfaffian; Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov and the BCS gap equation are its stationarity at first order, and its components are given by SuperfieldComponents). It is the Legendre transform of -log Z (W = log Z) with respect to the two-point source K (and, with "MeanFields", the one-point source J): stationary (FunctionalDerivative with respect to G) where G^-1 = G0^-1 - Σ[G] (Dyson, Σ = SelfEnergy[Phi, G]), and equal to -log Z (the grand potential over T) there. It is also called the Luttinger-Ward or Baym-Kadanoff functional Ω[G], and Γ[<phi>, G] of Cornwall, Jackiw and Tomboulis at zero mean field; some authors (Almbladh, von Barth and van Leeuwen) call this form the Klein functional and keep the name Luttinger-Ward for the form with Σ[G] inside the logarithm. A truncated Phi gives a Φ-derivable (conserving) approximation. EffectiveAction2PI[Z0, interaction, n, G0 -> G] takes Phi = LuttingerWardFunctional[Z0, interaction, n, G0 -> G]. The option "MeanFields" -> {phi -> phiMean} (one real boson) or {psi -> Psi, psibar -> Psibar} (fermions: Grassmann-odd means, zero on shell at zero sources; complex bosons {phi -> phiMean, phibar -> phibarMean}, the unbarred field being the one whose source is in the first slot of G0 in Z0, or the one not declared with the sign -1) or {NambuField -> X} (a superfield: one Grassmann-odd mean, the free part -1/2 X G0^-1 X) makes the expectation values of the fields variables too, declared as sources so that FunctionalDerivative differentiates with respect to them. EffectiveAction2PI[Z0, interaction, n, D0 -> G, "Statistics" -> "Boson", "MeanFields" -> {phi -> phiMean}] is then the 2PI effective action Γ[phiMean, G] of Cornwall, Jackiw and Tomboulis, S[phiMean] + 1/2 Tr ln G^-1 + 1/2 Tr(D^-1[phiMean] G - 1) + Γ2[phiMean, G]: S is the classical action, D^-1[phiMean] = D0^-1 + S_int''[phiMean] the bare inverse propagator in the background (phi^4: the mass lambda phiMean^2/2; the trace of S_int'' is written as the diagram <S_int^(2)>_G), and Γ2 is minus the 2PI vacuum diagrams with lines G and the vertices of S_int[phiMean + phi] of degree three or more in phi (phi^4: lambda phiMean phi^3/6 and lambda phi^4/24); the mean field enters Γ2 only through these vertices, and at phiMean = 0 it is Γ[G]. Its stationarity conditions are the field equation δΓ/δphiMean = S'[phiMean] + 1/2 S'''[phiMean] G + δΓ2/δphiMean = 0 and the Dyson equation with Σ[phiMean, G] = SelfEnergy of Γ2. At phiMean != 0 a diagram of Σ need not be 2PI as an open graph (the bubble with two vertices lambda phiMean, as in phi^3 theory): the perturbative Σ in the background is selected with SkeletonDiagrams, not with ParticleIrreducibleDiagrams[Σ, 2, ...]. For fermions Γ[Psibar, Psi, G] = -Psibar G0^-1 Psi + S_int[Psibar, Psi] - Tr ln(-G^-1) - Tr(G0^-1 G - 1) + <S_int^(2)>_G + Phi[Psibar, Psi, G], the vertices with an odd number of fluctuating fields carrying one mean: the Nambu-Gor'kov functional of the superfield (psi, psibar) at zero anomalous propagator, exact at zero means in the normal state (no pairing source and no spontaneous pairing; in a paired state the anomalous propagator is finite at zero means too); at finite means the anomalous propagator is needed (Gpsipsi ~ V Psi Psi), and the superfield functional ("Statistics" -> "Superfield", "MeanFields" -> {NambuField -> X}) at its stationary G is the 1PI action Γ[X], the anomalous diagrams included. For an interaction even in the fields (phi^4, the two-body interaction of fermions), where δ^2Γ/δphiMean δG = 0 at zero mean field, the derivatives with respect to the means at zero mean field and fixed G are skeleton vertex functions: the second is D0^-1 - Σ[G] (for fermions FunctionalDerivative[Gamma, Psibar[a], Psi[b]] = G0^-1(a, b) - Σ[G](a, b), the rightmost derivative acting first), the fourth the fully irreducible vertex Γirr ("FullyIrreducible" of ParquetDecomposition: the bare vertex, then the envelope from the fourth order; for fermions FunctionalDerivative[Gamma, Psibar[x1], Psi[x2], Psibar[x3], Psi[x4]] = Γirr(x1, x2; x3, x4) in the convention F(x1, x2; x3, x4) of PerturbativeFullVertex, irreducible in all three channels, and FunctionalDerivative[Gamma, G[x4, x3], Psibar[x1], Psi[x2]] = -Γ0(x1, x2; x3, x4); for a superfield FunctionalDerivative[Gamma, X[a], X[b], X[c], X[d]] = Γirr(a, b, c, d), and FunctionalDerivative[Gamma, G[a, b]] = -1/2 (Σ + G^-1 - G0^-1)(a, b)); "MeanFieldDegree" -> {k, ...} computes only the terms of these degrees in the means. In general (phi^3) δ^2Γ/δphiMean^2 at fixed G differs from G^-1 (for phi^3 it is D0^-1: the bubble of Σ[G] comes through the mixed derivative δ^2Γ/δphiMean δG), and the 1PI Γ^(2) is the Schur complement Γ_phiMeanphiMean - Γ_phiMeanG Γ_GG^-1 Γ_GphiMean. Its 1PI counterpart is EffectiveAction1PI. The option "Source" -> U adds a one-body source to the bare inverse propagator, so that the action gains ∫ (barred field) U (field): G0^-1 -> G0^-1 - U for fermions (∫ psibar U psi), G0^-1 + U for complex bosons (∫ phibar U phi), D0^-1 + U for real bosons (1/2 ∫ phi U phi), G0^-1 - K for a superfield (1/2 ∫ NambuField K NambuField: the one-body source and the pairing sources 1/2 ∫ psi Kpsipsi psi, 1/2 ∫ psibar Kpsibarpsibar psibar). Γ depends on U only through the trace term, so that by stationarity the derivative of the grand potential is the explicit one, δΩ/δU(x, y) = G(y, x) = <psibar(x) psi(y)> (<phibar(x) phi(y)> for complex bosons, 1/2 G(x, y) for real bosons): an expectation value is a variation, N = -∂Ω/∂μ for U = -μ δ. U must be a kernel: a single symbol is taken as one, so that a chemical potential is "Source" -> LabelFunction[-mu DeltaFunction[a, b], {a, b}] (or mu is put into G0). Its second derivative is the response of a Φ-derivable approximation, χ = γ L γ with L = L0 + L0 Γ0 L and Γ0 = δΣ/δG (ExactEquation "Response" and "Susceptibility"), conserving: its density response vanishes at zero momentum and finite frequency, and its static limit is the second derivative of Ω (EvaluateMatsubara, option "Limit"). EvaluateMatsubara evaluates Γ in momentum and Matsubara frequency, its traces included. Option "Method" as in PerturbativeCorrelationFunction, for the diagrams of Phi when it is computed from Z0.

nodes.name: EffectiveAction1PI
nodes.usage: EffectiveAction1PI[Z0, interaction, n, phi -> phiMean, D0 -> Dm] is the one-particle-irreducible (1PI) effective action Γ[phiMean] of a real boson to order n, the Legendre transform of -log Z with respect to the source of phi (the quantum effective action of Jona-Lasinio, the generating functional of the 1PI vertex functions; at constant phiMean the volume times the effective potential, Coleman-Weinberg at one loop): S[phiMean] + 1/2 Tr ln Dm^-1 - (connected 1PI vacuum diagrams with the vertices of S_int[phiMean + phi] of degree three or more in phi and lines Dm), with Dm = D[phiMean] = (D0^-1 + S_int''[phiMean])^-1 the propagator in the background, whose derivative with respect to phiMean is declared (DeclareFunctionalDerivative: dDm(x, y)/dphiMean(a) = -Integral Dm(x, u) S_int'''[phiMean](u, v, a) Dm(v, y)). FunctionalDerivative with respect to phiMean gives the exact equation for the mean field and, at phiMean = 0 (Dm = D0 when the interaction has no quadratic part), the vertex functions VertexFunction of ConnectedFunctionFromVertices: Γ^(2) = D0^-1 - Σ and Γ^(n) = -(amputated 1PI n-point function), whose skeletons are PerturbativeFullVertex: SetSourcesToZero[FunctionalDerivative[Gamma, phiMean[a], phiMean[b]]] /. Dm -> D0, then ExpandTrace (which contracts Dm . Dm^-1). With the lines Dm a derivative brings a coupling (dDm/dphiMean does), so that the derivatives of the action of order n hold terms of higher orders, not all of them complete: keep the orders up to n (OrderPart). It is the 2PI effective action EffectiveAction2PI[Z0, interaction, n, D0 -> G, "Statistics" -> "Boson", "MeanFields" -> {phi -> phiMean}] at its stationary G[phiMean]. With bare lines, D0 -> D0, the vertices of degree two in the fluctuation stay vertices: S[phiMean] + 1/2 Tr ln D0^-1 - (connected 1PI vacuum diagrams with lines D0 and the vertices of S_int[phiMean + phi] of degree two or more), the same series written in D0, the rings of the vertices of degree two being the one loop. For fermions, EffectiveAction1PI[Z0, interaction, n, {psi -> Psi, psibar -> Psibar}, G0 -> G0] is Γ[Psibar, Psi] with bare lines, its only form (the propagator in a Grassmann background has anomalous parts, as in Nambu-Gor'kov): -Psibar G0^-1 Psi + S_int[Psibar, Psi] - Tr ln(-G0^-1) - (connected 1PI vacuum diagrams with lines G0 and the vertices of S_int[Psibar + psibar, Psi + psi] of degree two or more, the anomalous V Psi Psi psibar psibar and V Psibar Psibar psi psi included). The means are declared as Grassmann sources; at zero means FunctionalDerivative[Gamma, Psibar[a], Psi[b]] (the rightmost derivative acting first) is G0^-1(a, b) - Σ(a, b) (the perturbative self-energy), and FunctionalDerivative[Gamma, Psibar[x1], Psi[x2], Psibar[x3], Psi[x4]] the full vertex F(x1, x2; x3, x4) with bare lines, whose skeletons are PerturbativeFullVertex. For a superfield, EffectiveAction1PI[Z0, interaction, n, NambuField -> X, G0 -> G0, "Statistics" -> "Superfield"] is Γ[X] with bare lines, -1/2 X G0^-1 X + S_int[X] - 1/2 Tr ln(-G0^-1) - (connected 1PI vacuum diagrams); its components (SuperfieldComponents) are Γ[Psibar, Psi]. Other lines for fermions and superfields, a single Grassmann field or complex bosons give the message onepi and $Failed. EffectiveAction2PI with "MeanFields" -> {psi -> Psi, psibar -> Psibar} at its stationary G is the Nambu-Gor'kov functional at zero anomalous propagator: to third order it differs from Γ[Psibar, Psi] by the diagrams with an anomalous vertex, which the superfield functional recovers.

nodes.name: TraceLog
nodes.usage: TraceLog[A] is Tr ln A, for an operator A: kernels (symbols h standing for h[x, y], or LabelFunction objects), numbers (times the identity), sums, coefficients times operators, products A . B (Dot), integer powers and inverses A^-1 (Inverse[A] is read as A^-1). Write A^(-1) . B: Mathematica reads A^-1 . B as A^(-(1 . B)), which is taken as A^(-1) . B with the message opdotpower. A source enters an operator through a kernel: a LabelFunction (the one-loop action 1/2 TraceLog[D0^-1 + LabelFunction[lambda/2 phibar[u]^2 DeltaFunction[u, v], {u, v}]] is differentiated with respect to phibar) or a head with a declared derivative; a source outside any kernel gives the message opsource. A single symbol is a kernel; in a product with Times the factor that contains a declared kernel (DeclareDirectedPropagator, DeclareSymmetric, a source, the variable of the derivative) is the operator and the others are coefficients (lambda S with S declared); when this cannot be told (lambda S with neither declared) a message is given and the result is $Failed.
